title: The days slip by
hook: the early saloks warn that days slip away while the mind sleeps (Salok M9, ang 1426)

segments.voice: Yesterday, gun, and your line: sing, while there's time. Did you sing or hum one line out loud? While there's time, it said. Today the saloks look straight at the time itself. Day five hundred ninety.

Look at a photo from five years ago. The haircut, the phone in your hand, the people beside you. Some of them you still see. Some you haven't spoken to in years. Where did those five years go? You were there for every day of them, and yet most of them have left no trace at all. It's not that you were asleep. You were busy. But busy can be its own kind of sleep. The early saloks of Guru Tegh Bahadur keep coming back to this, couplet after couplet, like someone gently shaking a sleeper's shoulder.
screen: `A PHOTO FROM FIVE YEARS AGO.` → `WHERE DID THE DAYS GO?` → `BUSY CAN BE A KIND OF SLEEP.`

segments.voice: The second salok asks, in paraphrase: why are you so absorbed in poisonous things? You don't turn away from them even for an instant. Says Nanak, meditate on the Lord, O mind, and you won't be caught in death's noose. The word for instant is nimakh, the blink of an eye. The salok isn't asking for a whole life of retreat. It asks: could you look up, even for one blink? The third salok ends with a line that sums up this whole run of couplets: your lifespan is passing, slipping away. Auadh is the span of life, the time you were given. And it's going, right now, at exactly the speed of this sentence. Listen to how the saloks repeat themselves, too. Again and again, the second line begins kaho naanak, says Nanak, and then calls the mind: O mind, man re, manaa. They are built like a refrain. That repetition is the teaching. A single warning gets forgotten by lunchtime. A couplet that keeps coming back, day after day, at the end of every reading, wears a groove in you. Notice what the saloks don't say. They don't say the days are bad, or that time spent working or loving is wasted. They say the days slip, and the mind sleeps through them. The cure isn't more hours. It's waking up inside the ones you have, even for the blink of an eye. That's why the practice today is so small. You don't need to change your life to notice it. You just need to look at the clock and really see it.
screen: `WHY SO ABSORBED IN POISON?` · `NIMAKH: ONE BLINK OF AN EYE.` · `AUADH: THE LIFESPAN SLIPPING.` · `KAHO NAANAK: A REFRAIN THAT WAKES.` · then, large: `THE DAYS SLIP.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice the time right now. Look at a clock, or your phone's time, and say it to yourself. Then say the date, the day of the week, and where you are. Now close your eyes. This is the only time there is. Feel the breath arrive and leave. Let each breath be a blink of waking, a nimakh. When you drift into plans or replays, come back to the clock's simple fact: it's now. If you pray, you can rest in Waheguru between breaths. The bell holds the time.
Auadh, the span of life. Guru Tegh Bahadur's early saloks warn that it is slipping away, and ask the mind to wake even for a blink.
Your line: the days slip. Today, three times, look at a clock and actually see it. Say the time, and take one awake breath. Day five hundred ninety.

screen: `DAY 590 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: NONE OF IT IS YOURS.`

howItsDone: Sikhs hear the ninth Guru's saloks at the close of every complete reading of the Guru Granth Sahib; many know their refrain, kaho naanak, by heart, and take them as reminders that life's time is passing.

match.prompt: the days slip by — tap the pairs.

myth: the saloks say time spent working or loving is wasted
they say the days slip while the mind sleeps; the cure is waking inside them.
the second salok asks the mind to turn away even for an instant
nimakh, the blink of an eye, is enough to begin.
many saloks repeat the same opening to their second line
kaho naanak, says Nanak, then a call to the mind.

fork.setup: the saloks say your lifespan is slipping away. what do they ask of the mind?
options: a whole life of retreat from the world.
to wake and remember, even for a blink.
to fill every hour with more tasks.
fork.reveal: the second salok asks why the mind won't turn away even for an instant, nimakh, and says meditate on the Lord, O mind.

trapdoor: what you thought: the days slip by is just a sad fact about getting older.
what it means: it's a wake-up call: the days pass whether the mind is awake or not, so wake, even for a blink.
what a scholar hears: the saloks work as a refrain, many second lines opening kaho naanak and turning to the mind, and that repetition, heard at the close of every reading, is part of how they teach.

sources.ref: Salok Mahalla 9, saloks 2–3 (Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1426)

notes: Paraphrase of salok 2 (bikhian sio kaahe rachio nimakh na hohi udaas; kaho naanak bhaj har manaa parai na jam kee phaas) and the second line of salok 3 (kaho naanak bhaj har manaa auadh jaat hai beet): please confirm wording, numbering and Ang 1426.
Day 597 (youth has gone) uses the first line of salok 3; this day uses only its second line to avoid overlap.
